item.title: China’s Soft Espionage: The Technology Transfers That Don’t Make Headlines
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Recently, our Georgetown team has been inundated with media requests for commentary on allegations involving the exposure of Nvidia chip technology and the implications for U.S. national security. These inquiries typically focus on how China’s intelligence services conduct espionage and what can be done to counter them.

We do not discount this threat. Espionage, cyber intrusions, and other clandestine activities are longstanding features of China’s efforts to acquire foreign technology. But our research over more than a decade suggests that these activities account for only a fraction of China’s overall foreign technology acquisition effort – probably not the largest fraction, and arguably not the most consequential.

Rather, China has created a whole-of-nation ecosystem that operates through a combination of legal transactions, illicit activities, and what we call “extralegal” transfers: arrangements whose details are unavailable to outside observers and whose legality cannot readily be established.

Because these less visible practices lack the sensational appeal of conventional espionage, they rarely receive comparable attention. The result is a distorted public understanding of China’s technology acquisition system and a misallocation of the resources intended to counter it.

Beyond Conventional Espionage

China’s pursuit of foreign technology is neither new nor mysterious. Since the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, Beijing has operated an elaborate infrastructure for identifying foreign technological advances, accessing them, and adapting them for domestic use.

The enterprise includes government ministries, scientific research institutions, commercial entities, technology transfer centers, professional associations, overseas laboratories, and programs designed to recruit scientists and engineers with specialized expertise.

Its antecedents extend further back, to China’s 19th-century efforts to acquire Western technology while preserving its domestic political and social institutions. Successive Chinese governments have formalized these efforts. The objective is not simply to copy inventions, but to leverage the knowledge to produce commercially and strategically useful results.

For analytical purposes, we distinguish among three broad categories of foreign technology acquisition.

Legal transfers include purchases of technology, foreign company acquisitions, joint research, investments in startups, overseas laboratories, university collaborations, and the recruitment of scientific personnel. These transactions are not inherently improper. Yet a transaction can be legal while also being a strategic risk.

Illegal transfers include traditional espionage, cyber theft, violations of nondisclosure agreements, theft of trade secrets, alleged “honey pot” operations, and other activities prohibited by law. These are the practices most familiar to the public, which media queries most frequently address – as in the case of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Extralegal transfers involve arrangements in which foreign technical knowledge is conveyed through channels that are not necessarily illegal but frequently opaque. Examples are undisclosed research affiliations, subsidized consulting, dual appointments, and the work of intermediaries whose relationships with China’s government are not apparent.

These categories are not exclusive. An otherwise legitimate collaboration may involve undisclosed conflicts of interest, while a commercial acquisition may be entirely lawful yet raise significant national security concerns.

Our concern is that the second category attracts disproportionate attention, while the first and third may facilitate transfers of equal or greater strategic consequence.

The Machinery Behind the Transfers

The scale and institutional character of China’s acquisition efforts distinguish them from isolated acts of industrial espionage.

One component is China’s science and technology intelligence (科技情报, STI) system. This network collects, analyzes, and distributes foreign technical information to domestic research and industrial organizations. Its civilian institutions include the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China, complemented by specialized organizations serving particular industries and defense requirements.

Another component is the ubiquitous “talent programs” – a network of organizations that identify and recruit overseas technical expertise. Chinese national and local authorities have sponsored numerous programs offering research funding, salaries, laboratory facilities, and other incentives to scientists and engineers working abroad.

Some arrangements involve permanent relocation to subsidized “commercialization centers.” Others permit researchers to maintain positions overseas while executing projects or consulting assignments in China. These include so-called “dual-base” (两个基地) arrangements, through which an individual may sustain professional activities in two countries.

Participation in such programs or in their global analogs – the Sino-U.S. (or Japanese, German, etc.) “professional associations” – does not by itself establish misconduct. That depends on the nature of the work, the information transferred, and whether participants comply with applicable disclosure requirements and contractual obligations.

Unlike a clandestine intelligence operation, much of this infrastructure is publicly acknowledged in Chinese government documents and institutional announcements. Its strategic significance lies not in secrecy alone, but in its organization, persistence, and cumulative effects.

Our research on China’s access to foreign artificial intelligence (AI) technology provides an instructive example.…

item.title: 18 Years After 26/11, Is India Finally Winning the War Against Terror?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

It is November 26 yet again, the anniversary of the 2008 Mumbai attacks. It’s a day when India not only relives one of the darkest chapters in its fight against terror but also has an opportunity to reflect back on how the fight against terror has evolved over time.

From a passive and often submissive strategy to a bold and highly kinetic strategy of “zero tolerance to terror,” the journey has been long but determined. A strong political resolve has aptly backed the armed forces in its sustained fight to dismantle the terror ecosystem, choke the support system, and bring terrorist forces to their knees, decisively. A brief glimpse of this was demonstrated during India’s response to the Pahalgam terror attack, which involved 88 hours of precision strikes into Pakistan in Operation Sindoor from May 7-10, 2025.

In recent weeks, another significant success was achieved in India’s fight against terror. On November 19, while addressing a counterterrorism conference in Delhi, India’s Home Minister Amit Shah hailed the security forces for eliminating the last known home-grown terrorist, Latif Bhat. Shah claimed that, with this success, the entire Kashmir has become free from India-born terrorists, marking a major milestone in India’s fight against terrorism. He added that India needs to further strengthen the concept of a proactive offensive approach in its counterterrorism policy, with a greater emphasis on enhancing structural and operational capabilities, to continue on this path.

As per data maintained by the South Asia Terrorism Portal, the number of terrorists killed in the current year is down to 25 from a high of 3,005 in 2001 and 1,232 in 2008. Similarly, casualties among the Indian security forces have dropped to four this year from highs of 883 in 2001 or 366 in 2008. Civilian casualties too have seen a drastic reduction with only two fatalities recorded this year against 1,508 in 2001 and 915 in 2008.

Does this mean that India has all but won its fight against terror? Does it mean that India can now focus more of its resources and thoughts on ever increasing threats on the conventional front? Has India’s multilayered counterterror strategy finally delivered the knock-out blow to cross border terror? Most of these questions do not have simple and binary answers and premature celebrations could undo years of hard work and sacrifices made by the armed forces.

A look back at how India’s counterterror strategy has evolved may offer answers to some of these questions.

Early Years of Terror Attacks: India’s Weak Response

Although the 26/11 terror attack in the financial capital of India, Mumbai, is often called India’s 9/11, India’s fight against terror truly started when cross-border terror from Pakistan commenced in Kashmir in early 1990s. Despite previous evidence, including captured documents, the direct role of Pakistan was first exposed with the hijacking of IC-814, an Indian Airlines flight, on December 24, 1999. Under huge public and international pressure – and also facing a lack of viable politico-military options – India agreed to release Pakistan based terrorists like Ahmed Omar Sheikh and Masood Azhar in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages.

The attack on the Indian Parliament in Delhi by Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), a Pakistan based terrorist group, on December 13, 2001 outraged India and led to a large-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram. Once again, under tremendous international pressure, especially as both countries had recently acquired nuclear weapons, the two-year stand-off finally ended without any direct punishment to Pakistan.

There were other terror attacks too, like the 2002 Akshardham Temple Attack, the 2006 Varanasi serial bomb blasts, or the German Bakery Blast in 2010 in Pune. In October 2005, 59 people were killed in serial blasts that rocked popular Delhi markets of Sarojni Nagar and Paharganj. Again, in September 2008, months before the Mumbai 26/11 attack, multiple blasts rocked commercial spaces of Delhi including Connaught Place, Greater Kailash and Karol Bagh. On September 7, 2011, a briefcase bomb exploded outside the Delhi High Court, killing 12 people, claimed by a terror group Harkat-ul-Jihad Islami (HUJI), affiliated with al-Qaida and largely based in Pakistan.

However, the 26/11 terror attack was nothing like anything seen before or since. Ten heavily armed terrorists, trained and dispatched from Pakistan through a maritime route, struck the heart of Mumbai. Over the next 60 hours, they attacked multiple locations, including the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Nariman House, and Cama Hospital. By the time the siege ended, 166 people had lost their lives, including foreign nationals and security personnel. The attack was a sad reflection of India’s preparedness to fight terror, and the sea route taken by the terrorists exposed yet another major gap in India’s strategy for fighting terror.

In all these cases and many more, India failed to respond directly and decisively against Pakistan, despite conclusive proof of its direct support in these attacks. How and when did India change its strategy?

The Kinetic Strategy

The swearing-in of the Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led government in May 2014 had a significant effect on India’s counterterror strategy. As the Modi government consolidated its power, the counterterror strategy too acquired a more muscular form. A growing and assertive India was no longer ready to gather evidence, compile folders, and present it to Pakistan or the international community.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-25 17:04 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Government set to double spending on social media unit to £25m
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Government set to double spending on social media unit to Â£25m

The budget for a government communications team which uses social media ads and influencers to reach the public has almost doubled since Labour came to power.

The New Media Unit, set up in 2024, is set to spend Â£25m this year on promoting government policies on YouTube, TikTok and other platforms, a Freedom of Information request by the BBC has revealed.

It comes as Andy Burnham was forced to defend his use of social media influencers to engage with young people, after a row over a video with explicit language that was recorded on the steps of 10 Downing Street.

The PM said the video was "not acceptable" and the creator of it, Max Balegde, had apologised and taken it down.

Burnham rejected calls from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to apologise for "debasing his office" and defended his strategy of appearing in influencer videos, arguing that was where young people got their information.

Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, was among about 60 content creators invited to Downing Street for a reception earlier this month.

The New Media Unit was not involved in the event on 9 November - but it has helped organise previous Downing Street receptions for content creators.

The FOI request reveals its budget has grown significantly in the two years since the unit was founded under Sir Keir Starmer, from Â£13.2m last year, to Â£25m this year.

It shows the unit's headcount has doubled too, from 21 employees last October to 43 today, as the government speeds up the shift towards digital communications.

The government says using digital platforms like TikTok, YouTube and Instagram is "the most cost-effective and direct way to reach many citizens, particularly harder-to-reach and vulnerable groups" who do not use traditional print, radio and TV outlets.

Most of this spending has been earmarked for "paid campaigns" online, with more than Â£8.8m spent since April.

Paid campaigns include using outside companies to push the government's priorities and messages in targeted adverts, which can take into account a person's age, gender, or location.

That could be inserting sponsored content on a person's social media feed in between posts from people they follow, or before a video on YouTube.

The FOI also reveals the unit has earmarked Â£750,000 for paying influencers to sell messages to their audiences, who may be mistrustful of a message coming directly from government.

One current campaign focused on the cost of living has paid content creators including Fisayo Martins, external, who runs a channel called Finance Matters UK on Instagram and TikTok, to advertise what support is available to citizens.

The Cabinet Office said the campaign has reached 13.2 million people on TikTok and 9.1 million people on Meta platforms, including Facebook and Instagram.

- Burnham defends inviting influencers into No 10 in PMQs row with Badenoch

Conservative shadow Cabinet Office minister Mike Wood said the government has "serious questions to answer about the use of of taxpayer-funded social media influencers to push the government's message".

"This spending on 'new media' exceeds anything seen under the previous government, yet transparency and accountability are nowhere to be found," he added.

The government said it was reducing overall spending on communications by streamlining operations and focusing the money on digital.

Over the past two years, as part of a wider overhaul, 39 media campaigns have been cancelled and 46 have had their budgets reduced, with some of the money saved going towards the New Media Unit.

The unit itself is in the process being absorbed into a new Government Media Unit according to a government spokesperson, which will apply the unit's approach.

While the unit predates Andy Burnham, he has embraced social media since becoming prime minister.

He regularly records his own content as well as collaborating with influencers, to tap into their audiences.

His "more social first" approach has helped him to become one of the most viewed UK politicians on TikTok, as well as being one of the most followed across social media platforms.

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-26 05:58 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: How Can Australia Secure Its Future?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

This week, Australian Foreign Minister Senator Penny Wong delivered a major foreign policy speech to the Australian Senate. The speech was titled “Securing Australia’s future in a changing world,” and it sought to outline how Australia can navigate and protect its interests amid the major geopolitical shifts that are currently taking place. In particular, she highlighted how Australia will continue to place the United States at the center of its security architecture, despite the major ideological shifts that have occurred under the Trump administration.

Wong identified six shifts that are currently driving the global environment.

The first is the rising threat and use of force and coercion, with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine the clearest case, but also China militarizing disputed features within the South China Sea. Following this is the second shift: great powers have rethought what they want from the international system and how they pursue it. Washington is reshaping how it thinks about its interests and Beijing is attempting to reshape the Indo-Pacific around its own interests.

The third shift relates to stronger middle powers, like India and Indonesia, alongside Japan and South Korea, bringing their economic, diplomatic, and military weight into the Indo-Pacific. It is a redistributing of power. The number of middle powers has expanded since the end of the Cold War and this is creating a new source of power on its own.

The fourth shift is that trade, investment, and supply chains that were once a constraint on conflict are now being deliberately used as levers of pressure. This is related to the fifth shift that technology is changing the nature of economic and strategic power. This is happening not only through emerging technologies related to energy, but also AI, which is disrupting systems faster than anything before it, and the foreign interference it enables is cheaper, faster and harder to spot.

The sixth shift Wong identified is that countries are now finding it harder to act together. Multilateral institutions are waning in both resources and trust, and consensus on any major issue is becoming more difficult to create.

In response to these shifts, Wong rejected both fatalism and nostalgia. Her answer is an Australian foreign policy that is active, adaptive, and ambitious, one built upon Four R’s: region, relationships, rules, and resilience.

While Australia has sought to expand and deepen its other relationships, Australia’s central security pillar remains its alliance with the United States. To many in Australia looking at the ideological and behavioral shifts of the U.S. under Donald Trump, this may be perplexing and disappointing.

Australia’s approach to this turn in Washington has been to muddle through. Wong acknowledged these ideological shifts, but stated that it doesn’t alter the fundamentals of U.S. power: its economy, its military, and its indispensable role in Indo-Pacific stability. Australia’s position is to convince Washington that the final point especially is in its interests, as it is central to Australia’s.

But Wong also said that the United States is a “vigorous democracy” able to remake itself and the direction of its foreign policy post-Trump is unknown. Canberra’s calculation has been that there will be a “swingback” following Trump’s presidency. The recent midterm results lend support to that calculation.

Regardless of how erratic the White House may currently be, Wong acknowledged that there are still a great number of assets that the alliance provides. It gives Australia advanced technology and intelligence it couldn’t acquire alone, and it strengthens Australia’s capability to help deter aggression in the region. The United States remains the largest source of foreign investment in Australia, and the critical minerals framework signed by the two countries last year is pivotal to Australia’s future prosperity.

Wong pushed back on those who say that Australia should abandon the alliance because of Trump’s behavior. The alliance is bigger than the current occupant of the White House, and leaving it behind would give up a central source of strategic weight just when Australia needs every source of influence it can get. It would mean fewer choices, more vulnerability, and less capacity to help sustain a regional balance that protects sovereignty. The reality for Australia is that there is nothing comparable to the alliance that would protect Australia’s interests any better.

However, this does not mean Australia should be solely reliant upon that alliance. Wong highlighted that Australia has created the Treaty on Common Security with Indonesia and enhanced security ties with the Philippines, Singapore, and Malaysia. Australia’s partnerships with Japan and India have significantly deepened, while defense industry ties with South Korea have been upgraded, and a free trade agreement with the European Union was concluded after eight years of talks. Meanwhile, Australia has established a range of new treaties throughout the Pacific, with a new deal signed with Solomon Islands just this week.

The purpose of Wong’s speech was to explain to an anxious public, which may look around at a world that feels unstable and uncertain, that Australia’s answer to this cannot be to retreat from the world. The only response is greater engagement to try and shape the changing world to Australia’s benefit.

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-25 13:58 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/how-can-australia-secure-its-future/

item.title: What Happened to the China-US AI Talks?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

Two months ago, as concerns about AI safety dominated American headlines, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng met in New York. Seven weeks earlier, more than 1,100 researchers and executives at leading AI labs had signed a petition asking the U.S. government to support an international effort to “deliberately pace the frontier.” An individual lab slowing progress would do nothing to stop other labs from racing ahead. All American labs slowing down would do nothing to slow Chinese labs. Only a China-U.S. agreement could end the race dynamics.

The September meeting between the two ministers took the first fitful steps toward cooperation. Both sides agreed to formalize a “U.S.-China AI Dialogues” process, to set up an “incident line” for AI events with national security implications, and to begin developing protocols for agreeing on the leading AI dangers. They also agreed to hold their next round of talks in Shenzhen in November.

That was widely seen as referencing the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which both Bessent and He attended. But no dialogue between the two took place.

The intervening two months have seen both sides pulled away from cooperation, with China moving to restrict exports of its AI technology and the U.S. administration embroiled in a scandal over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Despite the setback, He and Bessent are both likely to attend the G20 summit in Florida from December 18-19, providing another chance for progress on cooperation.

Since their meeting in September, neither side has announced concrete measures to implement any of the three planks. Instead, both the United States and Chinese governments have taken steps to limit each other’s use of technology. In October, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), over which He wields considerable influence, and the Ministry of Science and Technology published a draft revision of the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export that adds 23 AI technologies spanning large models, agents, compute clusters, and information processing. Should that draft be finalized, it could significantly reduce U.S. access to Chinese model technology just as American firms are increasingly using those models.

Bessent, meanwhile, is near the center of the fallout from revelations involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China, whose former executive Alice Huang reportedly had a longstanding affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. In a rare public dispute between Cabinet members, Bessent faulted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to add Megaspeed to the Entity List, a step he said Treasury and other agencies had favored for months.

The Monday before the APEC summit, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule, which BIS said was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, to curb Chinese remote access to U.S.-built chips in third-country data centers. MOFCOM responded in terse language to the decision, with a spokesperson declaring the rule “deviates from the important consensus reached by the two heads of state… China is strongly dissatisfied with this and firmly opposes it.”

Neither the Americans nor the Chinese issued an official explanation of why He and Bessent failed to meet in Shenzhen, as neither ever officially confirmed the meeting would take place (no official confirmation preceded the September meeting either). Sensitivity over the Huang affair, tension over new restrictions, or simply reprioritization may all have played a role.

But the relationship between the two negotiation leads seems to remain on solid footing. The AI safety side conversation in September was part of a larger discussion of economic cooperation focused on implementing an agreement reached in Busan in October 2025, under which China paused its rare earth export controls and pledged to buy American agricultural goods in exchange for U.S. tariff relief. After Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke with He on the same topic earlier this month, China extended its suspension of rare earth export controls and the US extended 178 tariff exclusions on Chinese goods.

The following week, Bessent spoke at the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations gala, where he was optimistic about China-U.S. cooperation on AI. The secretary said he expects the two sides to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before release and that they are “establishing a direct channel to ensure that either nation can promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving its SI [super intelligence, the administration’s term for AI] models.”

Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, for their part, briefly discussed AI and “agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” according to Bessent. While nothing suggests that statement will turn into a formal agreement, the continued discussion of AI safety gives hope that Bessent and He’s “AI dialogues” could restart at the G20 summit next month.

A sideline discussion there could name the negotiators responsible for ironing out the details of an incident line: defining “serious incident,” determining which agency or official is responsible for both initiating and receiving notifications, and confirming that the hotline is operational.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-25 13:41 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/what-happened-to-the-china-us-ai-talks/

Six members re-elected to Sark's Chief Pleas

Six sitting members have been returned to Sark's Chief Pleas after the Sark general election recorded its highest voter turnout in 20 years.

Members Helen Plummer, Patrick Dewe, Nick Moloney, John Guille, Karl Rang and Joseph PerrÃ©e were among the successful candidates following the 73.67% voter turnout.

They were joined by Andrew Leaman, Thomas Lalor, Helen Sturman and Elliott Osborn.

Sitting member Carol Cragoe lost her seat, while candidates TomaÅ¾ Slivnik, Alan McKendry, Charlotte Golding, Daniel Golding and Christian Bravery were also unsuccessful.

The 73.67% voter turnout came from an electoral roll of 395 people and was up 16 people on the last by-election.

Of the total votes, 7% were done by proxy.

There was one spoilt paper as voting took place in the Island Hall and grounds on Wednesday.

Nine of the seats are available for a four-year term and one seat for a two-year term, after one conseiller was deselected due to non-attendance at three consecutive statutory meetings of the Sark government earlier this year.

item.title: Koizumi Shinjiro Is the Defense Whisperer That Japan Needs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

How many countries can say that their defense minister hosts a leading podcast? While some politicians around the world appear as guests on popular programs, Koizumi Shinjiro juggles his duties as Japan’s sitting defense minister while releasing biweekly episodes. “Shinjiro Koizumi’s Podcast,” as it is titled, regularly ranks among Japan’s top three political podcasts, covering everything from the Self-Defense Forces’ (SDF) counterpiracy operations in Djibouti to his personal ginger pork recipe.

Through this platform and his broader public persona, Koizumi is gradually demystifying Japan’s defense establishment and helping the Japanese public make sense of what may be the country’s most complex security environment since World War II. In doing so, he is fostering a long-overdue, more informed public conversation about Japan’s defense policy.

Koizumi’s podcast did not begin with defense issues. Until October 2025, the program reflected his priorities as Japan’s agriculture minister – or self-declared “rice minister” – tasked with stabilizing rice prices. While he may not yet be Japan’s most seasoned defense official, Koizumi possesses what many of his predecessors in Cabinet posts have lacked: a gift for communication, good looks, youthful energy, and a charismatic personality reminiscent of his father, former Prime Minister Koizumi Junichiro. These qualities make him a prime intermediary between Japan’s opaque bureaucracy and the public, with the podcast offering an approachable medium for engagement.

The Japanese public most commonly associates the SDF with emergency response, dispatched in the event of an earthquake, flood, or other disaster at home or abroad. They are highly competent in this arena, delivering supplies and conducting search and rescue with remarkable speed and coordination. However, viewing the SDF primarily through the lens of disaster relief risks overshadowing what defending Japan may require of them – or the decisions the public must weigh about their capabilities and deployment.

Most of the Japanese public views the SDF favorably – 93.5 percent – making the public opinion climate conducive to fostering a better understanding of their actual responsibilities and Japan’s evolving defense priorities. Koizumi has pried open that door by showcasing the SDF’s various activities, including live-fire drills, joint exercises with the United States and other militaries, and participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. In doing so, he highlights their strategic importance and the real sacrifices made by SDF personnel. He occasionally shares messages from listeners who say his podcast has deepened their appreciation for the SDF, with some even reporting that it has inspired them or family members to enlist.

A similar pattern could help raise awareness of wider defense issues. In a geopolitical climate marked by China’s rapid military buildup, the possibility of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait, an unpredictable nuclear-armed North Korea, and growing uncertainty about the United States’ security commitment, Japan has no shortage of challenges on its doorstep.

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s administration has taken meaningful steps to bolster Japan’s defenses, including a push to revise the three strategic documents – the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program – by the end of this year. Defense spending may be hiked from just under 2 percent to 3.5 percent of GDP over the next five years, in line with updated U.S. demands of its allies. Perhaps even more stirring has been Takaichi’s suggestion that there may be “room to discuss” rewording Japan’s third non-nuclear principle of prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country. She has also indicated that the SDF’s potential acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines was under serious consideration, a move that would challenge the current legal framework governing the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

These developments echo Koizumi’s recent calls to break the taboo on debating nuclear weapons. In a country strongly tied to its pacifist tradition, the Takaichi administration’s position departs from the general public sentiment, which firmly supports upholding the three non-nuclear principles. And while Koizumi, on his own, is unlikely to move the needle on this sensitive issue, he is perhaps the best candidate among Japan’s high-ranking officials to facilitate its public discussion.

A prerequisite to seriously broaching the nuclear weapons debate, however, is greater public awareness of the security threats Japan faces. This is also crucial if the Takaichi administration is to realize its most ambitious goal of constitutional revision, which would require not only approval by both Diet chambers but also a national referendum.

Polling shows that the Japanese public overwhelmingly sees China as the biggest national security threat. A full grasp of the security reality, however, requires not only identifying adversaries but also recognizing the importance of forging closer partnerships with like-minded neighbors like South Korea. Although relations with Seoul remain complicated by deep-rooted historical issues, Koizumi frequently shares insights from his diplomatic engagements, speaking positively about his interactions with his South Korean and other counterparts. Such glimpses may help improve public perceptions of these partners and convey their strategic value over time.

Koizumi’s podcast avoids the jargon and over-formality often found in political commentary, inviting listeners to contemplate the future of Japan’s security rather than be lectured. The sincerity with which he repeatedly expresses his appreciation for the SDF and the civil servants in his ministry has proven to resonate with listeners.…
